newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila works on government, protest in Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Kabila works on government, protest in Kisangani.

text.p: Laurent Kabila worked on the eagerly awaited first government of the new Democratic Republic of Congo on Wednesday but in the city of Kisangani students protested in one of the first signs of popular opposition.

Officials said Kabila, whose forces toppled Zaire's veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko at the weekend, met his top advisers at his new riverside headquarters to discuss the make-up of the government and security.
Aid workers in the northeastern city of Kisangani said more than 100 students protested peacefully against the alleged killing by a Kabila soldier of a fellow student.
They shouted "Tutsis go home", aid workers added.

France, a long-time friend of Mobutu, "solemnly" reminded Kabila that it was his duty to protect foreign nationals after two Frenchmen were shot dead in the capital on Tuesday but French ministers dismissed the killings as isolated incidents.
French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain, meanwhile hinted that France might be prepaared to admit Mobutu, who has cancer, for medical treatment.

World powers, both sympathetic and sceptical, have been pressing for a broad-based government as a sign of Kabila's democratic good faith and a first step towards multi-party elections. He had promised to unveil the government by Tuesday.
"We want free and fair elections everybody should be proud of and participate in," Kabila's foreign affairs adviser Bizima Karaha told reporters. "We want a ... genuine democracy."
Karaha said the new leaders of Africa's third largest nation had no intention of being stampeded by international pressure into elections for which the country was not prepared.
But he dismissed suggestions that Kabila could turn out to be another Mobutu by embracing one-party, one-man rule. "It's impossible...We hate dictatorship," he said.
South Africa, which has taken a lead in efforts to nudge Kabila towards a peaceful democratic transition, announced plans to send experts to help him rebuild the shattered economy.

"It is clear that there is a continuing hope South Africa will contribute to, at least, giving advice as to what might be done to secure the future of this country," Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told parliament in Cape Town.

Kabila, 56, arrived in Kinshasa after dark on Tuesday from Lubumbashi, his provisional headquarters on the Zambia border. He has moved into the heavy guarded riverside residence of Mobutu's last prime minister.
Soldiers of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) captured Kinshasa on Saturday, completing a stunning seven-month drive from the eastern border.
Kabila's forces further consolidated their hold on the capital on Wednesday, when two senior general surrendered.

General Amela Lokima, military governor of Kinshasa and deputy armed forces chief-of-staff, and General Michel Elessi, commander of Mobutu's forces in the capital, turned up at a hotel and were taken away by security officials, witnesses said.

National radio, renamed Voice of Congo, said members of Kabila's alliance were "in consultation with political personalities, notably Etienne Tshisekedi", the most prominent member of the internal political opposition to Mobutu.

Mobutu, 66, remained in Togo's capital Lome after prolonging a technical stopover on health grounds. A source close to the government said he was "very weak" in arrival on Sunday from his jungle palace in north Zaire.
"We hope he can get the treatment that any sick person deserves," Godfrain told Reuters in France.
A growing list of nations have recognised Kabila as head of state. Cuba was among the latest. Western powers have generally voiced cautious backing, linking this to progress on democracy.
